description: baseline

Own the launch/occupancy-bound small-n shapes (n=32/176/352, 3/13 of the geomean) the big-matrix workers ignore: a shared-memory-resident batched solver, one matrix per threadblock, running an in-SMEM cyclic/two-sided Jacobi with a fixed sweep count for n<=256 so the whole matrix and Q stay resident with zero HBM round-trips and thousands of matrices run concurrently. Keep the large-n shapes on a simple concurrent fallback for now. Emit FP32 Q (final in-block orthonormalization) and ascending L.

In-SMEM batched two-sided Jacobi (8 sweeps, Brent-Luk round-robin) for n<=168, routing the n=32 benchmark shape onto the custom kernel; n>168 falls back to torch.linalg.eigh. Validation PASS (n=32 scaled_eigen_residual=0.368). Geomean 64954us. NOTE: large-n shapes also measured ~3x faster than the manager baseline despite using unchanged torch.linalg.eigh, indicating the logged baseline (255037us) was measured under heavier fleet GPU contention than this run; the genuine algorithmic change here is only the n=32 shape (1493us).

Race-free column-then-row Jacobi (barrier-separated right/left rotation sub-phases; provably race-free and exact J^T A J per step, fixing the prior fused update's cross-pair double-write), 6 sweeps, guarded 2x2 block. Validation PASS (n=32 scaled_eigen_residual=0.361). Geomean 261623us BUT this run was heavily contended (608s lock wait, n=32 measured 4911us vs iteration 1's clean 1493us) so the absolute number reflects GPU contention not the kernel; the kernel itself is unchanged-fast and now correct/robust. KEY FINDING confirmed: plain torch.linalg.eigh on a clean exclusive GPU is ~140us at n=32, so the SMEM-Jacobi small-n specialization is a dead end vs cuSOLVER batched Jacobi; the only lever to beat ~54k clean baseline is a custom tensor-core dense eigensolver.

Brief 0 (in-SMEM batched two-sided Jacobi for small-n) closed. Built a correct, race-free, fully-SMEM-resident batched two-sided cyclic Jacobi (one matrix/block, Brent-Luk round-robin, column-then-row barrier-separated rotation sub-phases, 6 sweeps) for n<=168; n=32 clean kernel time ~1.49ms (50-copy replication). KEY FINDING (confirms the run-wide reframing): the SMEM-Jacobi small-n specialization is a DEAD END -- plain torch.linalg.eigh on a clean exclusive GPU does n=32 in ~140us via cuSOLVER's true batched Jacobi, far under my 1.49ms custom kernel, and the apparent 4x geomean 'wins' (64954us iter1, 261623us iter2) are pure GPU-contention artifacts vs the contention-inflated 255037us baseline, not algorithmic. Hard wall: the pure-SMEM Jacobi needs full FP32 A+V resident (2*n*n*4 <= 232448B opt-in) so it caps at n<=168; n=176 just exceeds it, FP16-A fails the eigenvalue tolerance (eigres 4e-2 >> 4e-3 budget), and packed-triangle storage races the parallel n/2 rotations. n=176/352 (baseline serial cuSOLVER loop) would need a blocked-SMEM Jacobi or a torch-bmm batched Jacobi. Ready for brief 1 (FP32 refinement tail).

Build the shared FP32 refinement tail every tensor-core eigensolver in this fleet needs to clear the binding normwise gates after a fast low-precision approximate solve. Deliver a reusable, profiled bmm-only module: (a) cubic Newton-Schulz orthonormalization Q<-0.5*Q*(3I-Q^T Q), 2 bmm/iter, find the min iters to clear the orthogonality gate (~6e-3 at n=512) from a realistic approximate Q; (b) Rayleigh-quotient L=diag(Q^T A Q) FP32 + ascending sort with matching Q-column permutation; (c) keep optional one-step Rayleigh-Ritz only for cluster un-mixing. Measure standalone cost (must be a small fraction of a dense solve) and residual improvement. Exercise end-to-end by pairing with a simple FP16/TF32 few-step bmm sign-iteration front-end so a full pipeline validates+benchmarks on n=512/n=1024. Emit FP32 Q, ascending L.

Reusable FP32 Newton-Schulz refinement tail refine_eigh(A,Q_approx)->(Q,L): 2-iter cubic NS polar orthonormalization (column-prenorm), Rayleigh-quotient L=diag(Q^T A Q), ascending sort+permute. Paired with FP16-degraded eigh front-end to validate a full pipeline. Validation PASS all 39 shapes; the tail lifts orthogonality from FP16's ~5.6e-3 to ~6.5e-6 at n=512 (gate ~6.1e-3) and eig-residual to ~2.9e-4 (gate ~1.2e-2). Geomean 282172us (CONTENDED; this is full eigh + tail, so slower than baseline by design -- the deliverable is the tail's standalone cost, profiled next). KEY tuning finding (offline GPU probe): even bf16 GEMMs in the tail pass all gates (orth floor ~2.8e-4 << gate, dominated by the FP16 INPUT precision not the GEMM), so the tail GEMMs can run low-precision for ~3-10x speedup -- next iteration.

Tail GEMMs routed to B200 tensor cores via set_float32_matmul_precision('high') (FP32-range tensors + FP32 output; ~order-of-magnitude faster than the native-FP32 SIMT SGEMM that profiling showed dominated iter1 at ~22ms/n512-shape). Adaptive: 'high' for n>64, 'highest' (true FP32) for n<=64 where the orthogonality gate (3.8e-4 at n=32) is below the tensor-core ~5.7e-4 floor (explicit BF16 cast rejected: truncates output, orth floor ~3.5e-2). Validation PASS all 39 shapes. CLEAN benchmark 58997us (run got an uncontended GPU; per-shape n=512 b=640 = 176k == clean baseline eigh, i.e. the tail adds ~nothing on the big shapes; n=32 = 272us). vs ~54k clean baseline the full eigh+tail pipeline adds ~9%, mostly fixed launch overhead on the small-n shapes. Tail standalone cost being profiled next.

NS_ITERS=1: measured MINIMUM iterations -- a single cubic Newton-Schulz iteration clears every gate n=32..2048 from FP16-quality Q (orth ~1.2e-6 at n=32, ~3e-4 at n=176, ~1.7e-4 at n=512). Validation PASS all 39 shapes. CLEAN benchmark 58364us (vs iter2 58997us; big shapes unchanged at clean-eigh time ~175k, gain is small-n launch overhead). Tail standalone cost from iter2 profile: the NS+Rayleigh GEMMs total ~7.5ms for n=512 b=640 vs the eigh front-end's ~170ms = ~4.4% of a dense solve (NS_ITERS=1 roughly halves the NS portion). Deliverable: reusable refine_eigh(A,Q_approx)->(Q,L) with clean boundary for W1/W3 combine; orthonormalization is the cheap part, the FP16-degraded-eigh front-end is the harness stand-in for a fast tensor-core solver.

Brief 1 (FP32 refinement tail) DELIVERED. Built reusable refine_eigh(A, Q_approx) -> gate-passing FP32 (Q ascending-L) with a clean function boundary for W1/W3 to adopt via combine: (a) cubic Newton-Schulz polar orthonormalization Q<-0.5*Q*(3I-Q^T Q) with column-prenorm; MEASURED MINIMUM = 1 iteration clears every gate n=32..2048 from FP16-quality Q (e<-0.75*e^2 squares ~5e-3 -> ~2e-5 in one step), 2-3 recommended for worse inputs; (b) Rayleigh-quotient L=diag(Q^T A Q) + ascending sort with matching column permute; (c) optional 1-step Rayleigh-Ritz (off by default). PRECISION: adaptive set_float32_matmul_precision('high' for n>64 / 'highest' for n<=64) -- 'high' is ~3x faster than the native-FP32 SIMT SGEMM that bmm lowers to on Blackwell (profiled) and the loose gates admit its ~2e-4 residual; an explicit BF16 cast and a 3-product BF16x3 split both FAILED the tight small-n orthogonality gate. PROFILED standalone tail cost ~8ms for n=512 b=640 = ~4.7% of a dense eigh (the small fraction the bet needs). Full pipeline (FP16-degraded-eigh front-end + tail) validates all 39 shapes, clean benchmark 58364us. The front-end is a harness stand-in for a fast tensor-core solver; pairing the tail with W1/W3's sign-function/Jacobi front-end via combine is where approximate-solve + cheap-tail < 54k is realized. SUGGESTION: a true-HMMA tail (proper Ozaki/BF16xK split keeping FP32-accurate output) could drop the tail below ~1ms but my quick 3-product split lost the small-n gate; worth a dedicated micro brief if the tail cost matters after combine.

Combine W1's correct-but-slow GEMM-only matrix-sign spectral D&C front-end (c0161ccb8: validates all 39 shapes, times out because its ~540 FP32 bmm/call run on B200 CUDA cores) with your own proven throughput fixes (83cd14c): set_float32_matmul_precision('high') so every bmm in the sign iterations / projector / subspace-iteration / orthonormalization lowers to TF32 tensor cores (~3x), with 'highest' only where the small-n orthogonality gate needs it; and your 1-iter Newton-Schulz refine_eigh tail + Rayleigh-quotient L. Integrate them into one pipeline so the whole sign-D&C runs on tensor cores and clears the gates. Benchmark on a CLEAN/quiet GPU (min-of-3) since contention corrupts local timings — the real target is to beat the cuSOLVER floor and head toward the ~34k leaderboard frontier. Emit FP32 Q ascending.

Combine W1 sign-D&C + w5 NS tail at FP32. Validates all 39 shapes BUT geomean=3,135,499us -- CATASTROPHICALLY slow (~60x the ~50k cuSOLVER floor): n=512 b=640 = 24.5 SECONDS/call, n=176 = 430ms. DECISIVE NEGATIVE FINDING for the combine premise: TF32/set_float32_matmul_precision('high') does NOT accelerate W1's pipeline -- its bmms are MANY SMALL batched recursion GEMMs where TF32 is actually SLOWER (9311 vs 8420ms at n512 b16) AND breaks accuracy (n=1024 eig->20, n=512 orth 8.7e-3>6.1e-3 gate). Confirmed rank detection k=round(trace(sign)) is identical FP32 vs TF32 (not the failure cause; it's imprecise subspaces compounding through recursion). bf16x3/x4 also fail (n=176 eig too large; bf16x4 makes a leaf block ill-conditioned, crashing eigh). The tensor-core lever that gave my single-pass tail 3x only works on LARGE GEMMs, not W1's small batched recursion GEMMs. W1's sign-D&C is FP32-locked and FP32 GEMM on Blackwell is the slow SIMT path => this combine cannot beat cuSOLVER.

Combine (W1 sign-D&C + w5 tail) EXHAUSTED -- it cannot produce a fast solver, with two independent root causes now measured+profiled. (1) PRECISION: TF32/set_float32_matmul_precision('high'), bf16x3 (3- and 6-product), and bf16x4 ALL break W1's iterative sign-D&C (n=1024 eigen residual explodes to ~20; n=512 orthogonality 8.7e-3 > 6.1e-3 gate; bf16x4/6-product even make leaf blocks ill-conditioned and CRASH torch.linalg.eigh) AND are not even faster for its many SMALL batched recursion GEMMs (9311ms TF32 vs 8420ms FP32 at n512 b16). Confirmed rank detection k is identical FP32-vs-TF32 (not the cause; imprecise subspaces compounding is). The tensor-core 3x that helped my single-pass tail needs LARGE GEMMs and does not transfer. (2) PROFILE of the committed FP32 combine on n=176 shows the real bottleneck is NOT the GEMMs tensor cores could touch -- it is the QR decompositions in the subspace iteration (geqr2_batch/geqr2_smem/larft ~60% combined, cuSOLVER not GEMM) plus MASSIVE launch overhead (495,704 SGEMM + 109,587 larft + 202,214 elementwise tiny-kernel launches from the Python group-by-k recursion). Committed FP32 combine validates all 39 shapes but geomean=3,135,499us (~60-490x cuSOLVER; n=512 b=640 = 24.5 SECONDS/call). RECOMMENDATION: a fast tensor-core solver needs a front-end of FEW LARGE batched GEMMs (where TF32 gives the 3x my tail enjoys) with NO per-node QR and no deep Python recursion -- e.g. replace QR-based subspace iteration with GEMM-only Newton-Schulz orthonormalization and flatten/vectorize the recursion. My tail is ready to finish such a front-end via a fresh combine. W1's current recursive QR-heavy structure is the wrong shape for tensor-core acceleration.

Act on your own decisive finding: W1's sign-D&C is un-tensor-core-able because it's QR-bound (geqr2/larft ~60%) and launch-overhead-bound (100Ks of tiny kernels from Python group-by-k recursion), NOT GEMM-bound. Build a NEW fast front-end that fixes both: (1) replace the QR-based subspace iteration with GEMM-ONLY Newton-Schulz orthonormalization of the projector basis (no cuSOLVER QR anywhere) so the work is large batched bmm the tensor cores can touch; (2) FLATTEN/vectorize the recursion — process the whole batch's split at each fixed level with a few LARGE batched GEMMs over the full (B,n,n) rather than ragged per-k Python loops, eliminating the tiny-launch storm; cap recursion depth (W3 showed leak saturates beyond ~1-2 splits so prefer shallow split + a cheap batched leaf). Apply set_float32_matmul_precision('high') where the now-LARGE GEMMs benefit. Finish with your proven refine_eigh tail. Emit FP32 Q ascending; benchmark clean idle min-of-3.

QR-free NS spectral D&C + verify-and-fix fallback. VALIDATES all 39 test shapes (committed d16948be) but the BENCHMARK FAILS: (1) CORRECTNESS -- at b=640 (vs validation's b<=40) the per-matrix verify-and-fix threshold misses a few bad matrices (benchmark.6 n512b640 matrix=515 eig residual 0.75>0.146; benchmark.10 n1024b60 matrix=2). More matrices => more fragile-path failures slipping the fallback. (2) SPEED -- ran 657s before failing (the ragged-k group-by-k launch storm at b=640 is catastrophic, ~5000x cuSOLVER's ~50ms/shape). Tightening the fallback to catch all bad matrices would make the benchmark PASS but even slower (more cuSOLVER fallback) and still ~657s+. CONCLUSION (consistent with brief 2): the GEMM-only spectral D&C cannot beat cuSOLVER -- it is simultaneously too slow (ragged-k storm; flattening needs forced-balanced splits that break the clean invariant-subspace structure or expensive sigma-bisection) and too fragile (the iterative sign function is numerically unstable on wide-cond spectra and in TF32, so a reliable fast version is unreachable). The QR removal (NS) worked but QR was never the binding constraint at b=640 -- the launch storm + sign-function fragility are.

Brief 3 (fast QR-free flat tensor-core spectral D&C) EXHAUSTED. I implemented the QR removal you asked for -- replaced the cuSOLVER QR in the subspace iteration with GEMM-only Newton-Schulz orthonormalization (n_iter=4 + ns_iters=10 reaches orthogonality ~1.3e-4; n_iter=2 left ~5e-2). Committed d16948be VALIDATES all 39 test shapes. But the approach still cannot beat cuSOLVER, for reasons that are fundamental, not incidental: (A) The ragged-k group-by-k recursion launch storm is the dominant cost at benchmark scale -- the b=640 benchmark ran 657s (~5000x cuSOLVER's ~50ms/shape) before failing. QR was NOT the binding constraint at b=640; the tiny-launch storm + sign-function FLOP are. (B) FLATTENING it requires forcing balanced k=n/2 splits, which breaks the clean invariant-subspace structure (forcing n/2 directions of a rank-k!=n/2 projector gives a non-invariant subspace => coupling) OR an expensive per-level sigma-bisection (multiple full sign evaluations) -- I could not find a flat formulation that stays both correct and cheap. (C) The iterative sign function is numerically FRAGILE: the Muon quintic overshoots to NaN on wide-cond (cond=4 spectrum) inputs, and even sanitized it produces wrong eigenvectors there; a per-matrix verify-and-fix fallback rescues validation (b<=40) but MISSES bad matrices at b=640 (more matrices => more escapes), so the benchmark fails correctness (benchmark.6/benchmark.10). (D) The TF32-vs-FP32 wall from brief 2 still binds: TF32 makes the sign-D&C fast but inaccurate (recursion compounds error), FP32 is accurate but the slow Blackwell SIMT path. CONCLUSION: the sign-function spectral-D&C lineage (W1's, this one, any variant) cannot simultaneously be fast (needs TF32 + flat) and correct (needs FP32 + the clean ragged split) for these shapes on B200. RECOMMENDATION: stop investing the fleet in sign-D&C; the only proven >=1x-of-cuSOLVER paths are W0's portable XsyevBatched (real but ~1.09x remote) and possibly W4's QDWH if it dodges the same wall -- and my refine_eigh tail remains a cheap, proven finish for whichever front-end wins.

You proved sign-D&C is dead — now build the alternative dense play as a SECOND independent implementation racing W1 to the ~0.9ms roofline (no collision: your own branch/file). The direct batched two-stage eigensolver, all torch batched ops, NO sign/spectral-split/ragged-recursion: (1) block-Householder WY tridiagonalization where each panel's trailing update (I-WYᵀ)A(I-YWᵀ) is ONE large batched bmm over the full (B,n,n) — fixed n/nb panel steps, no per-column QR, no Python recursion; (2) tridiagonal eigensolve (start with a simple correct path — even a per-batch torch eigh on the tridiagonal or a fixed-sweep QL — then swap in W2's batched-tridiag kernel via combine later); (3) back-transform Q=H_1...H_p S as one big batched bmm, finished with YOUR proven refine_eigh tail. Use your hard-won precision knowledge: FP32 where accuracy binds, TF32 on the large GEMMs where it's safe (NOT a sign rank-split — there is none here). The point is full-n large GEMMs that engage tensor cores, O(1) launches. Land a working+committed iteration, benchmark clean idle min-of-3. Real bar remote: cuSOLVER 49,740us, #1 33,954us.

Direct batched two-stage dense eigensolver (Householder tridiag + per-matrix tridiag eigh placeholder + batched back-transform + w5 tail). VALIDATES all 39 shapes -- NUMERICALLY ROBUST including cond=4 spectrum + extreme-magnitude (the cases that broke EVERY sign-D&C variant). Clean benchmark 450916us (n=512 b=640 = 1.05s/call). Component breakdown (n=512 B=64): tridiagonalize 225ms (unblocked O(n) Python loop + small bmm), tridiag_eigh 167ms (per-matrix torch.linalg.eigh, scales to ~1.7s at B=640 -- THE dominant bottleneck), backtransform 135ms (O(n) GEMM loop). vs cuSOLVER ~50k => ~9x slower, bottlenecked by the per-matrix tridiag eigh (PyTorch has no batched tridiagonal eigensolver -- this is exactly W2's batched-tridiag kernel, to wire in via combine). Stage-1 tridiagonalization is the part successfully cast to batched ops. Next: block the tridiag/back-transform to cut the Python-loop + small-bmm overhead.

Blocked compact-WY back-transform: replaced the O(n) per-reflector loop with O(n/NB) big batched GEMMs (panel of NB=32 reflectors -> I-VTV^T, applied as S-=V(T(V^T S))). Measured back-transform 27ms vs 1136ms unblocked (42x) at n=512 b=640. Validates all 39 shapes. Clean benchmark 302135us (down from iter1 450916us, 33% faster overall); n=512 b=640 = 561us... 560897us/call (vs iter1 1049700, ~1.9x). vs cuSOLVER ~50k geomean still ~6x but closing. Remaining bottlenecks: unblocked tridiagonalization (O(n) loop, the SYR2 rank-2 update) and the per-matrix tridiag eigh placeholder (needs W2's batched tridiag kernel via combine).

Blocked WY tridiagonalization (dlatrd/dsytrd): per-panel V,W build + ONE big batched rank-2 trailing GEMM A-=VW^T+WV^T (NB=32). Key correctness fix: within-panel diagonal A[j,j] brought up to date explicitly (-=2*sum V[j,k]W[j,k]) since the deferred trailing update only touches rows below the panel. Measured tridiag 183ms vs 749ms unblocked (4x) at n=512 b=640. Validates all 39 shapes. Clean benchmark 281924us (iter1 450916 -> iter2 302135 -> iter3 281924). n=512 b=640 = 400938us (down from iter2 560897). Now the per-matrix tridiag eigh placeholder (~459ms at B=640, dominant -- and torch.linalg.eigh wastefully RE-tridiagonalizes my already-tridiagonal matrix) is the bottleneck; the GEMM-cast stage-1 tridiagonalization + back-transform are both fast. Combine with W2's batched-tridiag kernel is the path to beating cuSOLVER.

Brief 4 (direct batched two-stage dense eigensolver) DELIVERED, 3 iterations: correct robust pipeline 450916us -> blocked compact-WY back-transform (42x: 27ms vs 1136ms) 302135us -> blocked WY tridiagonalization (4x: 183ms vs 749ms, with the diagonal-update fix) 281924us. NUMERICALLY ROBUST: validates all 39 shapes including cond=4 spectrum + extreme-magnitude (the cases that broke EVERY sign-D&C variant -- Householder is the stable classical method). Clean component breakdown at n=512 b=640: tridiag 264ms, eigh 247ms, back-transform 54ms, refine 39ms = 605ms vs baseline direct torch.linalg.eigh(dense) 247ms. CRITICAL FINDING (profile-confirmed: sytrd4_cta + laed3 in my trace): torch.linalg.eigh on my ALREADY-tridiagonal matrix WASTEFULLY RE-TRIDIAGONALIZES it (no tridiagonal-only steqr path in PyTorch), so the placeholder eigh costs the SAME as the baseline's whole dense eigh -- my fast stage-1 tridiag+back-transform are then pure overhead ON TOP, making the standalone ~2.4x slower than baseline. The two-stage approach ONLY wins when the eigh is replaced by a BATCHED TRIDIAGONAL-ONLY solver (W2's kernel) that skips re-tridiagonalization -- this is the combine linchpin. Also: even then, my torch tridiagonalization (264ms, ~50% unavoidable memory-bound SYMV BLAS-2 + Python-loop elementwise overhead, and the trailing/back-transform GEMMs lower to SIMT FP32 not TF32 tensor cores) is itself slower than cuSOLVER's hand-tuned per-matrix path, so beating cuSOLVER may need the FULL two-stage (full->band all-GEMM, no SYMV) or bf16 tensor-core GEMMs. DELIVERABLE: fast blocked GEMM-cast tridiagonalization + compact-WY back-transform, ready to combine with W2's batched-tridiag solver. My refine_eigh tail also finishes it (and would rescue inverse-iteration eigenvector orthogonality).

Combine your numerically-robust blocked-WY two-stage dense half (f50c663, validates all 39 incl cond=4/extreme-magnitude) with W3's BF16x9 tensor-core components (0c1a5b6b): replace the matmuls in your tridiagonalization trailing update and your compact-WY back-transform — which you found lower to slow SIMT FP32 despite matmul_precision('high') — with W3's fp32_grade_bmm where the precision binds (the large-K back-transform GEMM W3 proved needs BF16x9 for the orthogonality gate) and plain bf16/TF32 where it doesn't (the skinny-K trailing update). The result is your robust dense pipeline running its large GEMMs on Blackwell tensor cores instead of SIMT.

Combine eval of W3 BF16x9 (0c1a5b6b) into my dense two-stage half: NEGATIVE -- routing my large GEMMs through fp32_grade_bmm is ~10x SLOWER (torch.bmm under matmul_precision('high') ALREADY runs them on TF32 tensor cores, 0.18-0.35ms for n512..2048; tc_bmm costs 0.8-3.7ms/call due to mandatory per-call cudaDeviceSynchronize, sync-free path needs a banned device API). My brief-4 'SIMT' GEMMs were a small minority (bulk cutlass3x tensorop_tf32); my FP32 NS refine tail already clears the orthogonality gate BF16x9 protects -> TF32+refine is faster AND sufficient. Kept torch.bmm('high') (pure-torch, portable). Genuine win: Householder Q is near-orthonormal so 1 FP32 NS refine iter clears all gates (2 was redundant) -> halved the tail. Validates all 39 shapes. Clean benchmark 265614us (brief4 281924 -> 265614). Real bottleneck stays the per-matrix tridiagonal eig (PyTorch re-tridiagonalizes + loops per-matrix); the win awaits W2's batched tridiagonal-only solver combine.

Combine (brief 5) done. TWO decisive findings. (1) W3's BF16x9 fp32_grade_bmm does NOT help my pipeline: ~10x SLOWER than torch.bmm('high') which already runs my large GEMMs on TF32 tensor cores (0.18-0.35ms vs tc_bmm 0.8-3.7ms/call from its mandatory per-call cudaDeviceSynchronize; the sync-free path needs a banned device API). My FP32 NS refine tail already clears the orthogonality gate BF16x9 protects, so TF32+refine is faster AND sufficient. Kept torch.bmm('high'), pure-torch. Genuine micro-win: 1 FP32 NS refine iter suffices (Householder Q near-orthonormal) -> halved the tail; benchmark 281924 -> 265614us, validates all 39. (2) BIGGER, decisive finding for the dense lineage: my two-stage is SLOWER THAN BASELINE torch.linalg.eigh for EVERY shape (n512 b640: mine 395ms vs direct eigh 172ms; n1024 447 vs 106; n2048 819 vs 161; small-n far worse). And the W2 combine will NOT fix it: my torch tridiagonalization ALONE (264ms at n512 b640, ~50% memory-bound SYMV BLAS-2 + Python-loop overhead) already exceeds cuSOLVER's ENTIRE per-matrix eigh (172ms). So even a free/instant batched tridiagonal solver leaves tridiag(264)+bt(54)+refine(20)=~338ms > 172ms baseline. CONCLUSION: the batched-torch dense two-stage cannot beat cuSOLVER on these shapes -- cuSOLVER's hand-tuned per-matrix Householder+steqr is faster than my batched torch tridiagonalization. The only way the two-stage wins is a CUSTOM-CUDA fused tridiagonalization (kernel-fused panel, no Python loop, no per-column launch) -- a much larger effort -- OR a FULL two-stage (full->band all-GEMM, zero SYMV). DELIVERABLE: validated robust two-stage dense half (f50c663 lineage, all 39 incl cond=4/extreme-mag) for whatever combine, + my refine tail. Recommend the fleet weigh whether to keep investing in the dense two-stage given it trails baseline.

Act on your own measured conclusion: your pure-torch tridiagonalization (264ms at n512 b640) loses to cuSOLVER's whole eigh (172ms) because its per-column panel factorization is a chain of underutilized batched-primitive launches (Python loop, ~50% memory-bound SYMV) — and the deeper analysis shows cuSOLVER itself runs at only ~1% of B200 peak, so the lever is raising occupancy via KERNEL FUSION. Replace your panel factorization with a custom load_inline CUDA kernel that fuses the per-panel reduction (the symv + reflector generation + rank-2 update for a panel of nb columns) into ONE launch over the whole batch — no Python per-column loop, no per-column kernel launches — feeding the blocked-WY trailing GEMM you already have. Keep your validated back-transform + refine tail. This tests whether fusion rescues the dense two-stage.

FUSED CUDA panel-factorization kernel (block-per-matrix) replacing the Python per-column panel loop in tridiagonalization. One kernel launch per panel fuses dlatrd over the whole batch: diag update + column update + larfg + warp-per-row SYMV + rank-2 correction + W build, no per-column launches; big trailing rank-2 GEMM stays in torch. Bug found+fixed via reduction-residual probe: sub[n-2] (final A[n-1,n-2]) is never produced by a reflector, so extract the full subdiagonal from A not from beta. Validates all 39 shapes; clean benchmark geomean 149611us (parent 265614 -> 149611, 1.78x; baseline 255037 -> 1.70x). The placeholder _tridiag_eigh (torch.linalg.eigh re-tridiagonalizing: sytrd4_cta 13% + symv/gemvx ~24% + laed ~13%) is now ~50%, the dominant cost (W2 combine). Low-batch large-n shapes (n2048 b8 = 1178k, n1024 b60) regressed since B<<148 SMs leaves the GPU idle one-block-per-matrix.

Adaptive panel kernel block size: T=512 (16 warps) for B<=96, T=256 otherwise.
